Theme

School & learning · Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

translate verb

also translation, translate into Latin, word for word, translate this sentence, translate from Latin to English, translate from English to Latin

classical

Plaut. Trin. 19: Plautus vertit barbarē
Cic. Fin. 1.7: sī plānē sīc verterem Platōnem
Traupman 32, 397
M-O s.v. translate

vertō, vertere, vertī, versum

verb, third conjugation

From one language into another: ex Graecō in Latīnum vertere (Liv. 25.39.12, Lewis & Short; Traupman 32). Plautus’s ‘barbarian’ is Latin, as a Greek would call it.

Other words

  • convertō, convertere, convertī, conversum — translate

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Opt. Gen. 14: nec convertī ut interpres, sed ut ōrātor (Lewis & Short); Cic. Off. 2.87 (Lewis & Short); Traupman 32, 249, 397; Traupman 34

    A translation is conversiō (Traupman 32) or interpretātiō (Quint. 2.14.2, Lewis & Short; Morgan–Owens).

  • trānsferō, trānsferre, trānstulī, trānslātum — translate, carry over

    verb, conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. Fin. 1.7: locōs quidem quōsdam, sī vidēbitur, trānsferam; Traupman 32, 249, 397; M-O s.v. translate

  • reddō, reddere, reddidī, redditum — render (in another language)

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 1.155: Latīnē redderem; Hor. Ars 133: verbō verbum … reddere

    Word for word is verbum prō verbō reddere (Cic. Opt. Gen. 14) or ad verbum exprimere (Cic. Fin. 1.4, Lewis & Short).

  • interpretor, interpretārī, interpretātus sum — interpret; translate

    verb, first conjugation, deponent · also used · classical · Cic. Fin. 2.20 (Lewis & Short); Quint. 8.6.44 (Lewis & Short); M-O s.v. translate

  • trānslātiō, trānslātiōnis f. — a translation

    noun, third declension · also used · classical · Quint. 1.4.18: sed haec vidētur ex συνδέσμῳ magis propria trānslātiō (of a term); Traupman 249, 397

    The rendering of a word or a text from another language (Quintilian; later Jerome, Augustine). In rhetoric it is also a metaphor (see figurative).

Examples

  • huic Graecē nōmen est Thēnsaurō fābulae: Philēmō scrīpsit, Plautus vertit barbarē

    In Greek this play is called The Treasure: Philemon wrote it, Plautus translated it into barbarianPlaut. Trin. 18–19

  • cum ea, quae lēgeram Graecē, Latīnē redderem, nōn sōlum optimīs verbīs ūterer et tamen ūsitātīs

    when I put into Latin what I had read in Greek, I used words that were not only the best but also familiarCic. de Or. 1.155

  • nec verbō verbum cūrābis reddere fīdus interpres

    nor will you take care, as a faithful translator, to render word for wordHor. Ars 133–134

  • ex Latīnō in Anglicum convertere

    to translate from Latin into EnglishTraupman 249

  • Converte (convertite) hanc sententiam ex Latīnō in Anglicum.

    Translate this sentence from Latin to English.Traupman 34

  • ex Latīnō in Anglicum (con)vertere

    to translate from Latin into EnglishTraupman 397
